rationale: No panel dissent is in the packet. The judgment changes in structure and at the margins, so a complete assessment is returned. Structure: the incumbent (a migration edition) adopts an assessment with no steelman, no per-claim treatments, no components and no research priority, all of which the method requires; every featured claim now carries a two-axis treatment. Margins: the fourteen previously featured claims keep their verdicts (TRN-C001 stays well_supported rather than established because TRN-E008 recovers eight of nine and TRN-E001 itself reports possible faint GTC counterparts it cannot exclude as chance). Four catalog claims are newly featured by stakes, not by evidence weight: TRN-C101 is the conventional account's core mechanism and must sit on the map beside the thesis; TRN-C102 is the rival reading of the case's pivotal shared measurement; TRN-C103 and TRN-C104 are the two remaining population rungs on which the near-Earth account stands. TRN-C101 is graded from the content of records linked to neighbouring claims (TRN-E002, TRN-E008, TRN-E011, TRN-E016, TRN-E024) and says so; TRN-C103 has no evidence record at all and is graded unresolved with low confidence on that ground rather than omitted. The load-bearing set gains TRN-C005 (the only geometric signature fallout cannot mimic) and TRN-C101. The crux order now leads with TRN-R003, because TRN-E024 reports that per-source microscopy is exhausted and the coma discriminant is the only physical incident-light test on the table; TRN-R010 (added to the ledger after the incumbent) follows TRN-R005; TRN-R001 is demoted to confirmatory; TRN-R009 is last as prospective only. Three accounts are supplied, matching the sections the article treats; the question is kept. The article keeps the founding narrative's voice and phenomenology but is rewritten to set the three accounts side by side with their predictions, to carry the four newly featured claims, to state what would change the verdict in both directions, and to drop statements not independently in the ledger: the gamma-ray-burst archival-search legacy, first names that appear only in the founding text, and the assertion that the discovery papers themselves acknowledged the fallout reading. The microscopy manuscript is described by its ledger status (arXiv preprint posted August 2026, unreviewed) rather than as 'shared ahead of publication'. The declined modelling and hotspot preprints failed quote verification and are not used; TRN-R010's summary carries a figure from a failed import, so the article describes that test without the number.
accounts: The marks are sub-second sunlight glints from reflective artificial objects near Earth, photographed before Sputnik (the VASCO thesis)

The marks are plate chemistry — emulsion flaws, copy-stage defects inherited by both digitizations, and scan artifacts — and the ensemble correlations are properties of an unvalidated catalog and the observing schedule (Hambly & Blair; Watters et al.)
The marks are real flashes from natural near-Earth bodies — icy dust aggregates trapped by the magnetosphere — so near-Earth light without anyone's hardware (Cann)
article:
On the night of April 12, 1950, the 48-inch Schmidt telescope on Palomar Mountain exposed a red-sensitive glass plate for about fifty minutes — routine work for the first great photographic atlas of the sky, made seven years before any nation had put a satellite into orbit. Decades later, researchers comparing that plate against everything photographed since noticed something odd: [nine star-like points, clustered within about ten arcminutes, that appear on that one exposure and on nothing before or since]{claim=TRN-C001}. Not on the overlapping plate taken six days later. Not in modern digital surveys that see several magnitudes deeper. Nine lights, one night, gone.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P01}

The project that found them — VASCO, for Vanishing and Appearing Sources during a Century of Observations, led by astronomer Beatriz Villarroel — went on to catalog thousands of such single-exposure candidates and to propose an explanation with a first-rate pedigree of strangeness: that some of these flashes are sunlight glinting off reflective objects near Earth, photographed years before Sputnik. That is the version that makes headlines. The [discovery paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-92162-7) is more careful than its retellings: its first-listed explanation is an unknown kind of plate contamination, and the reflector reading is offered only on condition that contamination can be excluded. That condition has never been met, and the whole dispute lives inside it, several rungs below the headline.

## Three ways to read a dot

Set the serious accounts side by side before weighing them, because they predict different things.

**Glints from hardware.** A reflective object at roughly geosynchronous distance catches the Sun for a fraction of a second and throws the light toward Palomar. The account predicts images sharper and rounder than the stars around them (a flash has no time to be smeared by the atmosphere), groups and lines of flashes on a single exposure from one tumbling body, a shortage of candidates inside Earth's shadow where nothing is sunlit, and — on the strong version — a population of artificial objects near Earth before October 1957 that no one has otherwise recorded.

**Chemistry.** Photographic emulsion makes dots without the sky's permission: holes, bubbles, development spots, handling damage, and flaws introduced when the original negatives were copied to glass positives and copied again. This account predicts that candidates concentrate toward plate edges and corners where defects congregate, that a flaw born at the copy stage is inherited by every dataset printed from it, that similar 'transients' turn up on the comparison plates too, and that any population statistics computed on an unvetted catalog track the observatory's schedule rather than the heavens.

**Real flashes from natural near-Earth bodies.** A third account, newer and thinner: the flashes are genuine and the objects are near Earth, but they are aggregates of charged cometary dust trapped by the magnetosphere — nature's debris, not anyone's satellite. It predicts the shadow deficit the hardware account predicts and adds a dependence on geomagnetic weather; it removes the reason to believe in pre-Sputnik hardware without removing the reason to believe in near-Earth light.

A dark-matter reading has also been offered. It takes the transients' reality as given and proposes nothing that bears on whether they are real, so it sits at the edge of the table as context.

What decides between the first account and the second is whether any mark was made by light passing through the telescope. What decides between the first and the third is whether the objects behave like manufactured reflectors or like ice and dust. The record holds a good deal on the first question and almost nothing on the second.

## What nobody disputes

Start with what the fiercest critics concede. N. C. Hambly — an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Edinburgh who helped build one of the two great digitizations of the Palomar survey — put his own institution's glass copy of the 1950 field under a microscope. The nine marks are there, physically, at the reported positions, and absent from the copy of the plate taken six days later. They are not scanner glitches or software errors. An [independent detection pipeline, built from scratch by an outside researcher, recovers eight of the nine — plus about two-thirds of the published 5,399-candidate catalog]{claim=TRN-C004}, at a cost of roughly one spurious detection per five control fields. And the 1950 event is not alone: [three point sources of about sixteenth magnitude, within ten arcseconds of one another, appear on a plate from July 19, 1952 and are gone from the next exposure taken within the hour]{claim=TRN-C003}; 2023 imaging with the Gran Telescopio Canarias to magnitude 25.5 finds nothing there, which means whatever flashed dimmed by more than ten magnitudes in under an hour and has stayed dark for seventy-one years.

So the marks are real features of the plates. The question is what makes a mark.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P02}

## The case for chemistry

[Ordinary emulsion, copying, and scanning flaws produce isolated star-like detections at rates high enough to contaminate any single-exposure transient search]{claim=TRN-C101}. This is not a skeptic's conjecture; everyone in the dispute works from it. Hambly's inspection turned up emulsion holes, bubbles, and scratch-like marks on both copy plates, and 'transients' on the comparison plate that were absent from the 1950 plate. The catalog-building paper removed 3,592 artifacts by comparing digitizations before arriving at 5,399 candidates. The independent pipeline, sweeping the whole survey footprint with preliminary settings, generated 2.85 million raw candidates — five hundred times the vetted list — a measure of how much 'the population' depends on who is doing the vetting. And the proponents' own 2026 machine-learning paper exists because reviewed image pairs had to be sorted by eye into real versus plate defect. What has never been measured is the base rate: how often each copying stage mints a fake star. That number is the conventional account's unpaid debt.

Hambly and his coauthor Blair added two sharper points. First, a measurement: [the nine 1950 marks are systematically sharper and more concentrated than real star images of the same brightness — all nine fall on the sharp side of the plate's profile distribution]{claim=TRN-C002}, a coincidence they put at roughly one in a billion if the marks were drawn from the stellar population. A classifier trained on confirmed stars, confirmed galaxies, and unmatched detections files the nine with the unmatched. Second, and structurally more damaging, a genealogy: the two modern digitizations that both show the candidates — whose agreement had seemed to rule out simple flaws — [descend from glass copies that share a common intermediate positive, so a single defect introduced at that shared copying stage would be inherited by both]{claim=TRN-C007}. 'It's in two independent datasets' turns out to mean 'it's in two cousins.'

{plate:IMG-TRN-P03}

That is the conventional account at full strength, and it is strong. Notice, though, what the classifier's training set does: its 'spurious' class is defined by having no modern counterpart — the very property that defines a transient candidate — so a population of genuine flashes would be labeled artifact-like by construction. The proponents press that circularity, and it is a fair objection. Morphology can group the nine with artifacts; it cannot show that any one of them is one.

## The case for light

The proponents' reply begins with physics. A star sits on the plate for the whole exposure, blurred by atmosphere and imperfect tracking; [a flash lasting under a second has no time to blur and should appear sharper and rounder than a star image]{claim=TRN-C102}. If so, the morphology argument points in either direction, or in none. The physics is sound as far as it goes; it is also uncalibrated. No one has exposed period-appropriate emulsion to controlled flashes beside artificial stars and drawn the curve, so no one knows whether flash profiles and defect profiles overlap entirely. And the record carries a wrinkle for a single-mechanism story of either kind: the most isolated of the three 1952 sources has a profile nearly identical to the comparison stars. The canonical events are not morphologically uniform.

The stronger development comes from outside the Palomar archive entirely. In 2026 I. Busko, a retired Space Telescope Science Institute developer, searched rapid same-night plate pairs from the Hamburg Observatory — [a different telescope, different emulsion stock, different archive, and a different digitization, where analogous appear-once candidates with narrow profiles duly show up]{claim=TRN-C010}. Hamburg's plates share no ancestor with Palomar's, so the copy-defect mechanism cannot reach them. The sample is 41 plates and the author calls it preliminary; there is no measured candidate rate against matched controls, so 'the same phenomenon' and 'the same susceptibility to defects' are not yet told apart. His follow-up went further. On a Hamburg reflector chosen because its parabolic optics stamp a strong comet-shaped distortion — coma — on any off-axis point of light, [candidate transient images reportedly carry the coma pattern expected of light that passed through the telescope]{claim=TRN-C011}. Scratches and chemistry do not know where the optical axis is; photons do. If that discriminant survives a blind test against known defects and deliberately produced flashes, the case changes character: it would be a physical incident-light detector usable on any plate archive. It has not been blind-validated, and the paper itself says the data do not establish where the light came from.

## The original glass

For decades every analysis in this dispute worked from copies, or scans of copies. In August 2026 a [preprint by J. Yang and Beatriz Villarroel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26371), not yet peer reviewed, reported the first microscopy of the original material: the glass negative that sat inside the Palomar Schmidt on April 12, 1950, examined at the Caltech plate archive, and a Harvard copy plate of the July 1952 field — each registered against the published digitization, star by star.

[All nine 1950 sources are present on the original negative at their published positions]{claim=TRN-C024}. They were not born in a scanner, and they were not born in the copying chain. The 1952 triple appears both on the copy plate and in the original survey digitization, which strands the copy-defect account for that event too. For the two flagship events, 'it's in two cousins' is answered with 'it's on the grandparent.' The genealogy argument keeps its full force against the hundred thousand uninspected catalog candidates and loses it exactly where the case is fought hardest — provided the registration holds up in review, which no one outside the group has yet checked.

And there the good news, for every camp, stops. Microscopy cannot tell a brief flash from a flaw born in the emulsion: at the single-source level the two produce the same sharp little dot, and the manuscript says so plainly. The microscopist who examined the Caltech plate — directed to the nine objects by Hambly himself — found them un-star-like and concluded that emulsion defects were a reasonable attribution, noting that the field lies in a corner of the plate, where defects are common. The authors print that opinion against their own interest and argue it embeds a default: judged against steady stars, a sub-second flash is supposed to look like a defect. Both readings of the same glass are correct as far as they go, which is exactly the problem. The one clean escape — the same flash caught from a second mountain at the same instant, yielding a parallax distance or nothing — is closed for these events; no simultaneous second-site plate of comparable depth exists.

So the crux is [whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope during the original exposure rather than introduced afterwards in the emulsion, the copying chain, or the scan]{claim=TRN-C020}. 'Original or copy?' now has a reported answer: original. 'Sky or chemistry?' does not, and per-source inspection cannot supply it.

## The statistics, honestly

Above the individual events sits an ensemble argument, and here the record is genuinely, instructively mixed.

The VASCO working catalog of roughly 107,875 candidates shows two celebrated patterns: [a deficit of candidates inside Earth's shadow at satellite altitudes — about 0.46 percent observed against 1.4 percent expected by geometry]{claim=TRN-C005}, where sunlit reflectors would go dark, and [elevated candidate rates within a day of atmospheric nuclear tests, a relative risk of about 1.45]{claim=TRN-C006}. Both patterns replicate. Both also fail to replicate. The difference is entirely in what 'replicate' means.

On the supporting side: B. Doherty, an outside statistician who began unconvinced, took the authors' 107,875 rows and independently written code and got both effects back — the nuclear-window risk at 1.45 with a permutation p of 0.006, the shadow fraction at 0.46 percent — with precipitation, moonlight and cloud-cover controls. (He afterwards joined the group, which strengthens the replication he did from outside and qualifies the work carrying his name since.) A 2026 machine-learning paper trained on 250 expert-labeled image pairs found the nuclear-window excess persisting among candidates scored likelier to be real, and the shadow deficit not only persisting but largest in the highest-probability subset. An open Bayesian reanalysis with public code, modeling temporal autocorrelation the original chi-square framing did not, keeps a one-day nuclear lag at p of 0.037 — attenuated, and outranked by a two-day lag on UAP reports. And one specific way of faking a temporal pattern has been tested and closed: across 12,510 Harvard exposures and 638 Palomar fields, plate sensitivity does not vary with geomagnetic activity.

On the undermining side: the [Watters critique](https://doi.org/10.1017/pasa.2026.10230) — written by researchers who take anomaly claims seriously — showed the shadow analysis assumes a uniformly random background the data visibly violate, with feature counts rising toward plate corners and edges and forming geometric clusters and voids; with a proper null there is no significant deficit. It traced the nuclear timing largely to the Palomar observing schedule, found that at least 91 percent of the features used had earlier been removed for lying within five arcseconds of catalog stars, and noted that a third of the reported linear-cluster features were never confidently distinguished from stars. The proponents answer that the critique's dataset is twenty times smaller than the working catalog, built for another purpose and underpowered — a genuine methodological dispute, not a resolution, since neither side's rows have been validated against star contamination and scan artifacts. Then the one fully independent reconstruction: Z. Hayes's pipeline, rebuilding a candidate catalog from the scans rather than accepting anyone's rows, finds a post-test relative risk of 1.35 that is not significant, and a null once nightly sky coverage is modeled as exposure. His catalog is noisy — about 7,250 candidates a night — so a weak real effect could be diluted; but the pattern is the tell. The correlations reproduce *conditional on the working catalog* and dissolve when the catalog is rebuilt. That does not prove they are artifacts. It proves the catalog is the battleground.

Two further population rungs are thinner still. [Candidate rates are reported to fall monotonically with geomagnetic activity, and controlling for it to strengthen the nuclear association]{claim=TRN-C103} — a single-author preprint on the same catalog, with no independent check. And [some multiple-transient events are reported to lie along straight lines, as point sources on a shared sky path would]{claim=TRN-C104}: seven plates carrying alignments of five to eight ML-scored sources at p below 0.03, the classic setting for look-elsewhere inflation (a pattern found after searching many plates with a criterion chosen afterwards), with Watters's warning that a third of earlier alignment members were not distinguished from stars.

Note too what the nuclear correlation could not establish even if it survived every test: radioactive fallout settling on photographic plates predicts it as well as glinting objects do, and nothing in the correlation itself excludes that mundane reading. The shadow deficit is different. Fallout does not know where Earth's shadow is. Of all the ensemble claims, it is the one with a geometry only a sunlit near-Earth population predicts, and that is why its fate in an independently built catalog matters more than any other statistic in the case.

## The ladder

Climb it and watch the support thin. That the marks exist on plate material: settled, by the critics themselves. That they are reproducible by independent software: settled. That the flagship nine are on the original negative: reported, pending review. That the population statistics mean anything: contested at the level of dataset definition. That any mark was made by light through the telescope: unresolved — the crux, and every rung above it is conditional. [That the light came from objects near Earth, at geosynchronous-like distances]{claim=TRN-C021}: unresolved, resting on the contested shadow geometry, and shared by the natural-aggregate account. [That artificial objects were near Earth before Sputnik]{claim=TRN-C022}: the headline claim, unresolved, and not selected even by a vindicated shadow deficit, since ice and dust cast the same shadow as hardware. [That they were extraterrestrial artifacts]{claim=TRN-C023}: presently untestable — no observation on the table bears on it, and even a proven pre-Sputnik object would need a separate origin argument before that word earned its place.

## What would change our mind

The research agenda follows the ladder. First, a blind test of the coma discriminant: freeze the classifier, feed it known stars, deliberately produced flashes, and the full defect bestiary with labels hidden, and read the confusion matrix — the single test that could certify or close a physical incident-light detector. Second, a flash-profile calibration on period emulsion, which would turn the shared sharpness measurement from direction-ambiguous into diagnostic, whichever way it falls. Third, the catalog: an open, from-scratch reconstruction of the working set, followed by a preregistered shadow analysis run across independently built catalogs with the heterogeneous-background objection built into the null. A deficit that survives that would be the best geometric evidence the near-Earth account could have; a deficit that does not would retire it. The nuclear correlation deserves a preregistered exposure denominator from raw plate logs and a leave-one-night-out check, since a rate effect and a couple of anomalous plates look identical in a contingency table. Independent archives need measured candidate rates against matched controls, not examples. The copying chain needs a defect census — how often each generation mints a star. A blinded outside repeat of the Caltech registration would ratify or break the original-glass result. And for any transient that happens again, two stations imaging the same field at the same instant would turn one ambiguous dot into a distance or a dismissal — the measurement no one can add to 1950.

What would move the verdict toward light: coma validated blind, the shadow deficit reproduced in a catalog nobody's thumb has touched, flash profiles calibrated to match the nine. What would move it toward chemistry: a measured copy-stage defect rate that accounts for the catalog, the coma signature failing its blind test, the nine's morphology matched by known emulsion flaws under calibration. Until one of those arrives, the honest verdict is neither.

assessment.synthesis: The case is bottom-heavy: the observation rung is as secure as photographic evidence permits, and everything above it is argued rather than measured. The nine 1950 marks are physical emulsion features confirmed by the critics on the Edinburgh copy (TRN-E002), recovered by an independent pipeline (TRN-E008), and reported present on the original Caltech glass (TRN-E022). That last record removes the copy-chain defect route (TRN-C007, TRN-E005) as an explanation for the two flagship events (TRN-E023) if its registration survives review, but it does not settle the crux: TRN-C020 narrows from 'original or copy?' to 'flash or flaw in the original emulsion?', and the manuscript's authors concede microscopy cannot decide that, with their own microscopist leaning defect (TRN-E024). The conventional mechanism (TRN-C101) is well supported as a pathway by records linked to neighbouring claims but has no measured base rate. Sharpness (TRN-C002) is credible and weakly diagnostic: both camps read the same measurement (TRN-E003, TRN-E004, TRN-E006) their own way, no controlled flash calibration exists, and the 1952 triple's star-like profile (TRN-E007) spoils a uniform story for either side. The ensemble claims split cleanly by replication type — they survive reanalysis of the author-supplied rows (TRN-E010, TRN-E015, TRN-E019) and fail independent extraction and a corrected null (TRN-E009, TRN-E011) — a pattern that indicts the catalog rather than the sky. The only physical discriminant on the table is the Hamburg coma signature (TRN-E014), unvalidated. The attribution rung inherits all of this; TRN-E020's natural icy-aggregate route means even a vindicated near-Earth geometry would not select the artificial branch, and nothing bears on extraterrestrial origin. Sensitivity: no single record's removal changes the case verdict, which is robustly unresolved; the record whose removal most changes the shape of the case is TRN-E022 — without it TRN-C024 collapses to untested and the copy-chain hypothesis regains full reach over the canonical events — with TRN-E011 second, since without it the two ensemble claims would rise from mixed to provisionally supported.
assessment.steelman: The strongest argument for the thesis that this assessment does not answer is the direction of the machine-learning stratification (TRN-E015): among the 107,875 candidates, the Earth-shadow deficit is largest in the subset scored most likely to be real, and the highest-probability candidates are the ones most concentrated in nuclear windows. A pure-defect population has no reason to know where Earth's shadow falls, and no reason for its likelier-real members to know it better than its likelier-fake members; the artifact account predicts the opposite gradient or none. Add that the phenomenon recurs, with the same narrow profiles, on Hamburg plates that share no ancestor with Palomar's (TRN-E013), that a subset there carries the off-axis coma pattern only light through the optics should produce (TRN-E014), and that both canonical multiplets are on original or original-digitization material (TRN-E022) rather than born in copying — and the proponents can say that every test yet applied that could have gone against them has gone their way, while the negative results (TRN-E009, TRN-E011) concern catalogs the critics themselves did not validate. The assessment's reply — that the ML labels are expert judgments on the same disputed imagery and that the whole analysis stays inside the contested catalog — is a provenance objection, not an explanation of the gradient. That gradient stands unexplained.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least some single-exposure, star-like detections on pre-Sputnik photographic plates — including nine on one April 1950 exposure and three on one July 1952 exposure — are genuine optical flashes recorded through the telescope; on the strong version of the hypothesis, they are sunlight reflections from artificial objects near Earth before October 1957.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether the marks exist — critics physically confirmed the canonical nine on surviving glass, and the proponents report them on the original negative — but one rung up: whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope during the original exposure rather than being a flaw born in the emulsion, a question per-source microscopy has now been shown unable to answer. Above that, whether any ensemble signal (Earth-shadow deficit, nuclear-test timing, geomagnetic dependence, linear alignments) survives independent catalog construction rather than merely independent re-analysis of the same contested rows; and, if any near-Earth signal survives, whether the objects are manufactured or natural.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: Blind-validate a physical incident-light discriminant — the coma-aberration signature, or a calibrated flash-profile curve on period emulsion — and apply it to the canonical Palomar marks; that would establish or exclude real flashes. Then reproduce the Earth-shadow deficit in candidate catalogs built independently from the scans under a preregistered, spatially heterogeneous null; that would begin to establish a sunlit near-Earth population. Artificiality would still require a behavioural or physical signature the ledger does not yet contain, and extraterrestrial origin would require more than that.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Photographic archives manufacture star-like marks without any sky event: emulsion holes, bubbles and development spots, handling and copying damage, and — critically for POSS-I — defects on the shared intermediate positive from which both major digitizations descend, so that one copying flaw appears 'independently' in two modern datasets. The critics' own inspection found such blemishes on both copy plates and 'transients' on the comparison plate too; the catalog pipeline removed thousands of artifacts and still describes its working sample as heavily contaminated; the microscopist who examined the original 1950 negative found the marks un-star-like and in a defect-prone plate corner, and judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution. On this account the ensemble correlations are properties of an unvalidated working catalog and the Palomar observing schedule, the candidate population's spatial statistics (edge and corner concentration, geometric clusters and voids) are the signature of plate and scan artifacts, and the sharpness of the nine is the sharpness of defects. Its unpaid debts are quantitative and specific: the star-like defect rate per copying stage has never been measured; it has no ready explanation for the machine-learning gradient in the shadow deficit; and the Hamburg candidates with reported coma signatures sit outside its simplest form.

researchPriority.reason: Several tractable, preregisterable tests exist at desk or lab scale with decisive information gain: a blind confusion-matrix test of the coma discriminant, a flash-profile calibration on period emulsion, and a from-scratch catalog reconstruction feeding a preregistered shadow analysis. Each would move the crux or retire an ensemble claim outright, and the coma test in particular would yield a tool usable across every historical plate archive regardless of how this case resolves.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim depends on TRN-C020 and TRN-C021, both unresolved. The only records bearing on it directly are TRN-E018 (weak, qualifying: alignments among ML-scored candidates on the same contested catalog) and TRN-E020 (weak, qualifying: a natural near-Earth mechanism that would explain the same geometry without hardware). Nothing in the ledger distinguishes manufactured reflectors from natural aggregates; the claim is an inference from the lower rungs plus the absence of known human launches, and the lower rungs do not yet hold.

treatment.plainLanguage: Human-made or otherwise artificial objects were orbiting near Earth before the first satellite, and they are what the plates photographed.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis. If established it decides the case; but it cannot be established by any observation currently in the ledger, because the geometry that would support a near-Earth population is shared with a natural account.
treatment.strongestObjection: Even if every lower rung held, the ledger contains no observation that distinguishes hardware from ice and dust, and the natural-aggregate account (TRN-E020) explains a sunlit near-Earth population without invoking anything no one launched.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The crux. Undermining: TRN-E004 (classifier files the nine with artifacts, though its spurious class is defined circularly) and TRN-E011 (no feature in the ensemble datasets shown to be an optical transient). Qualifying: TRN-E006 (flashes should be sharp — an uncalibrated physics argument) and TRN-E024 (microscopy of the original negative cannot separate flash from flaw, and the microscopist leaned defect). Supporting: TRN-E014 (coma on Hamburg candidates, unvalidated, not Palomar). TRN-E021 is context. No validated discriminant has been applied to any Palomar mark; the claim is neither established nor excluded.

treatment.plainLanguage: At least one of these marks was made by real light coming through the telescope that night, not by a flaw in the emulsion, the copying, or the scanning.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Everything above this rung is conditional on it; it is the exact dividing line between the chemistry account and both light accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only person to examine the original 1950 glass under a microscope found the marks un-star-like and judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution, in a plate corner where defects congregate (TRN-E024); and the strongest published reanalysis found no feature in the ensemble datasets demonstrated to be a transient (TRN-E011).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blind validation of the coma discriminant and its application to Palomar-like material (TRN-R003)
A flash-profile calibration on period emulsion showing the nine match flashes and not defects, or the reverse (TRN-R002)
A copy-stage and emulsion defect census giving a measured base rate for sharp clustered marks (TRN-R007)

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record is linked to this claim; the grade rests on the content of records linked to neighbouring claims and is stated as such. TRN-E002 reports emulsion holes, bubbles and scratch-like marks on both copy plates and 'transient'-like detections on the comparison plate absent from the 1950 plate; TRN-E016 records 3,592 artifacts removed from the vetted catalog; TRN-E008 shows a reasonable independent extraction yielding 2.85 million raw candidates against 5,399 vetted; TRN-E011 finds feature counts rising toward plate corners and edges and 91% of ensemble features earlier removed as star-adjacent; TRN-E024 has the microscopist attributing the nine to defects common in that plate corner. The proponents' own artifact classifier (TRN-E015) presupposes the claim. Not established because the base rate per copying stage has never been measured (TRN-R007).

treatment.plainLanguage: Old photographic plates routinely carry dots that look like stars but are chemistry or damage, often enough to swamp a search for one-night-only objects.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Opens the mundane pathway and sets the prior; it does not by itself close any specific mark or account for clustered multiplets on the original negative.
treatment.strongestObjection: A pathway is not an occurrence: no one has measured how often each generation produces sharp, star-like, clustered marks, and the Hamburg coma results (TRN-E014), if validated, would show that at least some candidates are not defects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A per-generation defect census yielding a measured rate for star-like marks (TRN-R007)
Blind coma validation showing most single-exposure candidates carry optical signatures (TRN-R003)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E005 (strong) documents the contact-printing chain: DSS and SuperCOSMOS are independent scans of independent copy negatives printed from the same intermediate positive. TRN-E023 (moderate, qualifying) does not dispute the genealogy but reports that both canonical events appear on original or original-digitization material, so the mechanism's reach over those two events is removed if the registration survives review. The claim as a mechanism stands; its diagnostic use against the flagship events is what has narrowed.

treatment.plainLanguage: The two modern digital versions of the survey are not independent witnesses: both were copied from the same intermediate glass, so a flaw on that glass shows up in both.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: High against the roughly 100,000 uninspected catalog candidates; now low against the two canonical events, which are reported present above the shared stage.
treatment.strongestObjection: It establishes a pathway without a rate, and the two events where it mattered most are reported on the original negative and original digitization (TRN-E022, TRN-E023).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A copy-stage defect census measuring how often star-like marks are born at the intermediate positive (TRN-R007)
Independent verification — or failure — of the Caltech registration (TRN-R001)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E001 (discovery), TRN-E002 (strong: critic-side physical inspection of the Edinburgh copy confirms all nine at the reported positions and their absence six days later), TRN-E008 (strong: independent pipeline recovers eight of nine), TRN-E022 (present on the original glass). Held short of established because one of the nine is not recovered by the independent pipeline and the discovery paper's own deep GTC imaging shows possible faint counterparts it cannot exclude as chance projections.

treatment.plainLanguage: There really are nine star-like marks on that one 1950 plate, at the positions claimed, and nothing is there on other plates or in modern surveys.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Common ground: both the chemistry and the light accounts predict marks that exist on the glass and are absent elsewhere. Their existence anchors the case but decides nothing between the accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: The same inspection that confirmed the nine found similar detections on the six-day-later plate absent from the 1950 plate, and a visible blemish population on both (TRN-E002) — existence of such marks is exactly what chemistry predicts.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent registration that fails to find one or more of the marks on the copy or original material
A confirmed modern counterpart at any of the nine positions

claimAssessments.reasoning: A single record, TRN-E022 (moderate): microscopy of the original April 1950 negative at Caltech, registered against the digitization with field stars as fiducials, finds all nine present. The manuscript is an unreviewed preprint, the examination was performed by the proponent group and was not blinded, and no outside party has repeated the registration. TRN-E024, from the same source, concedes that presence on the original does not decide the marks' nature.

treatment.plainLanguage: The nine marks are on the actual glass that was in the telescope in 1950, not just on later copies.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Removes the copy-chain defect route for the flagship event but leaves the flash-versus-emulsion-flaw question exactly where it was.
treatment.strongestObjection: One unblinded registration by the hypothesis's proponents, unchecked by anyone else; a registration offset could map copy-defect positions onto ordinary features of the original emulsion.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blinded outside repeat of the Caltech registration with published images (TRN-R001)
Peer-reviewed publication with the registration analysis exposed
Failure of any independent attempt to locate the marks on the original

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E003 (strong) carries the measurement: all nine profile statistics fall on the sharp side, with a joint probability of order 0.1 to the ninth if drawn from stars. TRN-E022 reports the marks marginally sharper than stars on the original glass. TRN-E004 and TRN-E006 are rival readings of the same measurement, not disputes of it. The measurement is common ground; its meaning is not.

treatment.plainLanguage: The nine marks are noticeably crisper and more compact than real stars of the same brightness on the same plate.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Sharpness is what emulsion defects look like and, by the physics argument, what sub-second flashes should look like; with no controlled calibration the direction it points is unknown, and the 1952 triple's star-like profile (TRN-E007) complicates any uniform reading.
treatment.strongestObjection: Both accounts predict it; a measurement both sides can claim discriminates nothing until a calibration curve exists.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A flash-profile calibration on period Schmidt emulsion (TRN-R002)
Profile statistics measured directly on the original negative rather than the copy lineage

claimAssessments.reasoning: The record bearing on this claim, TRN-E006, is linked to TRN-C002 and TRN-C020 and is a physics argument, not a measurement; the grade leans on priors — the optical reasoning that a sub-second event does not integrate seeing and guiding blur is straightforward — and is stated as such. TRN-E022 reports the original-glass marks marginally sharper than stars, consistent with it. Against uniform application: TRN-E007 reports the most isolated 1952 source with a profile nearly identical to comparison stars. No calibration exists.

treatment.plainLanguage: A flash lasting less than a second should look sharper than a star that sat on the plate for fifty minutes being smeared by the air and the telescope's tracking.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If calibrated, this converts TRN-C002 into a discriminant; uncalibrated, it merely makes the sharpness observation ambiguous rather than favourable to either side.
treatment.strongestObjection: The size of the effect relative to defect profiles is unknown, so flash and defect distributions may overlap entirely; and the 1952 triple is not sharper than its stars.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Controlled sub-second flashes on comparable emulsion producing profiles that match — or fail to match — the nine (TRN-R002)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E007 (moderate, peer reviewed) with 2023 GTC follow-up to magnitude 25.5; TRN-E008 (strong) recovers all three independently; TRN-E022 reports the triple on a Harvard copy plate and in the original survey digitization; TRN-E018 (weak) qualifies by extending the alignments line. The original 1952 negative has not been physically inspected.

treatment.plainLanguage: Three bright points appeared together on one 1952 plate and were gone from the next exposure less than an hour later, and nothing has been seen there since.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Existence is common ground; the event's constraints — more than ten magnitudes of dimming within an hour, star-like profile, three sources within ten arcseconds — are what any account must accommodate, but they do not choose between chemistry and light.
treatment.strongestObjection: Three marks within ten arcseconds on one exposure is also what a local cluster of emulsion flaws produces, and no one has examined the original 1952 negative.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Physical inspection of the original 1952 negative and its copy generations (TRN-R001)
A validated profile or coma analysis of the three sources
A confirmed counterpart at the position

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E008 (strong): a from-scratch pipeline with no reference to VASCO software recovers eight of nine 1950 sources and three of three 1952 sources, and matches 63.9% of the 5,399 published candidates at a median 0.94 arcsec; TRN-E016 supplies the catalog-construction context. Independence is of extraction, not of material: the pipeline reads the same DSS scans.

treatment.plainLanguage: An outsider's software, written without looking at the team's, finds the same marks and most of the same catalog.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Confirms the marks exist on the scans and are not products of one team's software — which neither account disputes — while showing that the candidate population is extremely sensitive to extraction choices.
treatment.strongestObjection: Same digitized descendants of the same copies; recoverability of a physical mark is expected whether it is a flash or a flaw.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A full open reconstruction of the working catalog that fails to reproduce most of it (TRN-R004)
A calibrated reprocessing that sharply changes the match fraction

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting: TRN-E010 (moderate; 0.46% in the umbral cone against about 1.4% expected, on the author-supplied rows), TRN-E015 (moderate; deficit persists and is largest among highest-probability candidates), TRN-E017 (moderate, indirect; plate sensitivity does not vary with geomagnetic activity). Undermining: TRN-E011 (strong; the uniform-background assumption is false, feature counts rise toward corners and edges, and with a proper null there is no significant deficit). TRN-E012 (weak) contests the critique's dataset size. The effect reproduces on the working catalog and has not been tested in an independently built one; the split is by replication type.

treatment.plainLanguage: Fewer of the candidate flashes fall in the part of the sky where a satellite-altitude object would be in Earth's shadow and could not reflect sunlight.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Of all the ensemble claims this is the one with a geometry only a sunlit near-Earth population predicts — fallout on plates cannot mimic it — so if it survived a preregistered test on an independent catalog it would be the best evidence the near-Earth account could have. Its current standing is conditional on an unvalidated catalog.
treatment.strongestObjection: The deficit vanishes when the spatially heterogeneous background is modeled (TRN-E011), and at least 91% of the features used had earlier been removed as lying within five arcseconds of catalog stars.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered shadow analysis across at least three independently constructed catalogs with the heterogeneous-background null built in (TRN-R005)
An open reconstruction of the working catalog (TRN-R004)
The deficit appearing, or failing to appear, in the independently extracted Hayes-type catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting on the author-supplied rows: TRN-E010 (relative risk 1.45, permutation p = .006, weather controls), TRN-E015 (persists after ML artifact scoring), TRN-E017 (one confounder closed), TRN-E019 (weak; survives a temporal-autocorrelation model, attenuated). Undermining: TRN-E009 (strong; independent extraction with nightly coverage as exposure gives a null), TRN-E011 (strong; insignificant after normalizing by observation days, largely determined by the observing schedule). TRN-E012 (weak) rebuts on power. Direction-ambiguous even if real: fallout deposition on plates predicts it as well as glinting objects do.

treatment.plainLanguage: More candidate flashes were recorded on the nights just before and after atmospheric nuclear tests.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a surviving correlation would not separate the accounts: radioactive contamination of plates and a near-Earth reflector population both predict it, and a handful of anomalous plates could produce it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The one fully independent catalog shows no significant effect once sky coverage is modeled (TRN-E009), and the timing tracks the Palomar schedule (TRN-E011).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered exposure denominator from raw plate logs (TRN-R008)
A leave-one-night-out test showing the association is a rate effect rather than the signature of one or two nights (TRN-R010)
The effect surviving in an independently constructed catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: The ledger holds no evidence record for this claim: the source that reports it (SRC-CANN-2026) is indexed but no record was extracted, and sources are not evidence by themselves. TRN-E017 and TRN-E020, by the same author, presuppose it rather than test it. With nothing to weigh, the grade cannot rise above unresolved, and this reflects the state of the ledger rather than a judgment on the correlation.

treatment.plainLanguage: Fewer candidate flashes were recorded on nights of strong geomagnetic activity, and allowing for that makes the nuclear-test pattern look stronger.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If real, a dependence on space weather is awkward for chemistry — plate sensitivity does not vary with it (TRN-E017) — but it does not separate artificial from natural near-Earth bodies, and it is computed on the same unvalidated catalog.
treatment.strongestObjection: Single author, unreviewed, same 107,875 rows; the strongest independent reanalysis attributes the catalog's temporal structure to the observing schedule (TRN-E011).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Extraction of the source's results into an evidence record and independent replication on a rebuilt catalog
Survival or failure under a preregistered exposure denominator (TRN-R008) and leave-one-night-out testing (TRN-R010)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E018 (weak, qualifying; linked to TRN-C003 and TRN-C022) reports seven plates carrying alignments of five to eight ML-scored sources exceeding Monte Carlo expectation at p < 0.03, with a post-hoc alignment criterion and no preregistered trials accounting. TRN-E011 reports that a third of the earlier linear-cluster features were not confidently distinguished from catalog stars. The alignments paper (SRC-VILLARROEL-2025-PASP) was not read in full and has no evidence record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the one-night flashes on a single plate line up in straight rows, as if one moving object had flashed several times along its path.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Genuine alignments among verified non-stellar point sources on one exposure would favour a moving body over scattered defects; but linear scratches and dust trails also make lines, and star contamination inflates any alignment count.
treatment.strongestObjection: Look-elsewhere inflation from searching many plates with a criterion chosen afterwards, plus unremoved catalog stars among the aligned members.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered alignment test on an independently constructed catalog
Alignment members verified as non-stellar on original material
Consistent angular rates along an alignment matching a single moving source

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E013 (moderate): rapid same-night pairs from the Hamburg 1.2-m Schmidt, digitized by APPLAUSE, show appear-once candidates with systematically narrow profiles; 41 plates from 1954–1957; the author labels it preliminary. No false-positive calibration, no injection-recovery test, and no matched-control rate. The result escapes the Palomar copy genealogy but does not yet separate a shared phenomenon from a shared susceptibility to defects.

treatment.plainLanguage: The same kind of one-night star-like marks turn up on old plates from a completely different telescope and archive in Germany.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Places the phenomenon outside the Palomar copy chain, where TRN-C007 cannot reach; but without a control rate, old emulsion failing the same way everywhere explains it equally well.
treatment.strongestObjection: Emulsion defects are universal; finding star-like one-night marks on another archive is what chemistry predicts too.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A measured candidate rate against matched control plates with injection-recovery completeness (TRN-R006)
The same search on further archives with published defect rates

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E014 (moderate): on 532 plate pairs from the Hamburg 0.6-m reflector, chosen for strong off-axis coma, candidate images reportedly show the coma pattern of off-axis point sources imaged through the optics. Single author, unreviewed; the classifier is not blind-validated; defect classes with directional asymmetry have not been excluded; the paper itself says the data do not establish the origin of the light; it applies to Hamburg candidates only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the German-plate candidates show the little comet-shaped smear the telescope's mirror gives to real light arriving off-center — a shape a scratch or chemical spot has no reason to have.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If validated, this is a physical incident-light detector: it decides flash versus flaw per candidate without needing original negatives or parallax. Unvalidated, it is a promising report.
treatment.strongestObjection: No confusion matrix exists; asymmetric defects (directional scratches, development streaks) could mimic coma, and the classifier was not frozen before labels were known.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind validation against known stars, deliberately produced flashes and the full defect bestiary, with the confusion matrix published (TRN-R003)
Application of a validated discriminant to Palomar-analogue material
Failure of the discriminant on known defects
